title: The Resurrection and the Life
sum: Jesus' friend Lazarus is sick in Bethany, near Jerusalem. Jesus waits two days, then goes back to Judea, though the authorities there have just tried to stone him. Lazarus has been in the tomb four days when he arrives. Martha meets him on the road, and in their talk Jesus says, "I am the resurrection and the life" (11:25), and Martha confesses him as the Messiah, the Son of God. Mary comes and weeps, Jesus is angry and shaken, and he weeps too (11:35). At the tomb he gives thanks to the Father and calls, "Lazarus, come out here!" The dead man walks out, still bound in his grave clothes.

This is the last and greatest of the signs in John's Gospel, and it turns the story toward the cross. Many believe, but some report to the Pharisees. The council meets, afraid that Rome will destroy the temple and the nation, and the high priest Caiaphas says it is better for one man to die for the people. John hears in his words a prophecy: Jesus will die for the nation and for God's scattered children. From that day the council plans to kill him. Jesus withdraws to Ephraim, and Passover draws near.
readings: The story is full of exact detail: a named family, a village under two miles from Jerusalem, four days in a rock tomb, a council meeting led by a known high priest. Read this way, the raising of Lazarus is the event that brought Jesus' conflict with the Jerusalem authorities to its crisis, as John says (11:53; 12:9–11, 17–19). Readers who take it so must explain why Matthew, Mark and Luke never mention it (see the deep dive).

John calls Jesus' miracles "signs": they point beyond themselves. Read this way, Lazarus coming out of the tomb shows what Jesus' words in 5:25–29 and 11:25–26 mean: those who hear the Son's voice pass from death to life now, and the dead will rise at his call. The irony is the heart of the chapter: by giving life, Jesus seals his own death, and by his death he gives life to others (11:50–52).
Read as a story of friendship and grief

Few chapters show Jesus so human. He loves this family (11:5), weeps at the grave (11:35), and is angry at death. Martha and Mary say the same words of grief and faith (11:21, 32). Read this way, the chapter is a pastoral text: it does not deny grief but places it beside a person who is the resurrection. It is read at Christian funerals more than almost any other passage.

views.H: Bethany lay on the Jericho road just over the Mount of Olives, and pilgrims for Passover passed through it. The chapter fits Jewish burial and mourning customs (same-day burial, seven days of mourning, wailing at the tomb) and the politics of Judea under Rome, where the high priest and his council answered to the governor for public order. Caiaphas held office from about AD 18 to 36, and his family tomb may have been found in 1990.
views.C: Many critical scholars think the raising of Lazarus was developed from older material: a miracle story from a signs source, Luke's sisters Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42), and perhaps the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, which ends with someone rising from the dead and still not being believed (Luke 16:19–31). They see in its placement John's own design, replacing the temple incident as the cause of Jesus' death. Others, such as C. H. Dodd and Richard Bauckham, argue that John drew on independent tradition with real historical memory.
views.L: This is the seventh and climactic sign, and the hinge of the Gospel: the "Book of Signs" (chapters 1–12) ends and the "Book of Glory" (chapters 13–21) is about to begin. Misunderstanding drives the dialogue (sleep and death, 11:11–14), irony fills the council scene (Caiaphas the unwitting prophet), and the fifth "I am" saying (11:25) stands at the center. Lazarus' exit with his grave clothes looks ahead to Jesus' empty tomb, where the wrappings are left behind (20:5–7).
views.J: Martha's faith in the resurrection on the last day is mainstream Jewish faith, especially among the Pharisees. In this chapter "the Jews" are mostly sympathetic mourners, many of whom believe (11:45). The council's fear of Rome was well founded, and Caiaphas' logic matches later Jewish debates about handing over one person to save a town. Jewish readers such as Adele Reinhartz note that this chapter shows the many faces of "the Jews" in John, and also how the council scene was later used to blame the Jewish people as a whole for Jesus' death.
views.T: The church read this chapter as proof of both natures of Christ: he weeps as a man and raises the dead as God (Leo the Great's Tome, AD 449, used a similar pairing). The Eastern churches keep Lazarus Saturday, the day before Palm Sunday, as a pledge of the general resurrection. 11:25–26 opens the funeral services of many churches, including the Book of Common Prayer.

deep.h: Why do the other Gospels not tell this story?
deep.b:
The raising of Lazarus is the greatest sign in John and the trigger for Jesus' arrest (11:45–53; 12:9–11, 17–19), yet Matthew, Mark and Luke never mention it. Scholars answer in several ways.

  • The other Gospels had different aims. They tell almost nothing of Jesus' visits to Judea before his last week and organize the ministry around Galilee. They do report other raisings (Mark 5:35–43; Luke 7:11–17). On this view, they left out a Judean event, as they left out the wedding at Cana and the man born blind.
  • Protective anonymity. Richard Bauckham argues that the early Jerusalem tradition behind Mark kept quiet about Lazarus, and left the woman who anointed Jesus unnamed (Mark 14:3), because the authorities had wanted Lazarus dead (12:10). When John wrote, late in the century, the danger had passed.
  • A story shaped by John. Many critical scholars (Bultmann, Lincoln, and others) think John or his tradition developed the story, perhaps from a simpler miracle account and from Luke's material about Martha and Mary and the parable of Lazarus, to show that Jesus' gift of life led to his death.

All agree that John made the story the turning point of his Gospel. Whether it happened as told is, for historians, a question about miracles in general as much as about this text. Believers and skeptics weigh it according to their wider judgment about the Gospels and about God.

deep.h: The Jews, the council and the blame
deep.b:
11:47–53 shows a meeting of "the chief priests and the Pharisees" deciding that Jesus must die. John says why: they feared that a popular messianic movement would bring Roman troops, and they would lose "our place and our nation" (11:48). The text describes a decision of a few leaders under Roman rule, not of a people. The same chapter shows many Jews grieving with the sisters and believing in Jesus (11:19, 31, 45).

Later Christian readers often ignored those distinctions and used the council scene, with 19:7 and Matthew 27:25, to blame all Jews of all times for Jesus' death. The Catholic Church rejected that charge at the Second Vatican Council (Nostra Aetate 4, 1965), as have most other churches. John's own theology also cuts against it: for John, Jesus lays down his life of his own accord (10:18), and he dies "for the nation" and for all God's children (11:51–52).

deep.title: Claude's theory: two tombs answer each other
deep.b: This is my own reading, though parts of it are close to what Brown, Lincoln and others say about the parallels. John seems to tell the Lazarus story and the empty tomb of Jesus as a matched pair, with each detail turned around. Both tombs are caves closed by a stone (11:38; 20:1). At Lazarus' tomb Jesus asks where the body has been laid (11:34); at his own tomb Mary Magdalene asks the same about him (20:2, 13, 15). At both, a Mary weeps, and the same verb is used (11:31, 33; 20:11). Lazarus comes out still bound, with a face cloth; Jesus leaves his linen and his face cloth behind, the cloth rolled up by itself (11:44; 20:5–7). Others must take the stone away and untie Lazarus; at Jesus' tomb the stone is already gone and no one helps him. My suggestion is that John means the reader to measure the second scene by the first: Lazarus was brought back to a life that would end again, but Jesus has passed through death to a life that does not end. That would explain why John is so careful about the cloths in 20:5–7.

settings.what: Jesus' words to the disciples about Lazarus' sickness and death
settings.to: his disciples, with him beyond the Jordan where John had baptized (10:40)
settings.when: after the sisters' message arrives, and two days later as he decides to go back to Judea
settings.why: To prepare the disciples for what is coming. He tells them the sickness serves God's glory, answers their fear of the Judeans with the proverb of the twelve hours (his time is in the Father's hands), and tells them plainly that Lazarus is dead, "now you can come to believe" (11:15). Thomas' reply shows that they expect the trip to end in death, as it nearly will.
settings.readers: For the Gospel's readers late in the first century, who knew that following Jesus had cost lives, Thomas' "Let's go as well, so we can die with him" (11:16) was a call they could recognize: loyalty that does not yet understand, but goes anyway.

settings.to: Jesus, staying beyond the Jordan where John had first baptized (10:40)
settings.when: while Lazarus was sick, a day's journey from Bethany
settings.why: The message makes no request; it only names the need and the bond: "The man you love is sick." It trusts Jesus to know what to do. Knowing that Judea had just tried to stone him (10:31, 39) shows what the sisters were asking him to risk.
settings.readers: For the Gospel's readers the sisters' message became a model of prayer that lays a need before Jesus and leaves the answer to him.

settings.what: Jesus and Martha on the road: "I am the resurrection and the life"
settings.to: each other, alone on the road outside Bethany, before Jesus enters the village
settings.when: four days after Lazarus' burial, during the days of mourning
settings.why: Martha speaks grief, hope and faith together: Jesus could have prevented the death, and God still listens to him. Jesus leads her from a hope placed on the last day to a hope standing in front of her. His words are meant to draw from her a confession of who he is, and they do (11:27). Knowing that these words were first spoken to a grieving sister on a road, not in a debate, shapes how they are heard.
settings.readers: Readers late in the first century, perhaps around Ephesus, were burying their own dead while still waiting for the Lord's coming. Jesus' words to Martha assured them that believers who die will live, and that the life he gives does not end at death.

settings.what: Martha's call to Mary, Mary's words to Jesus, and the mourners' remarks
settings.by: Martha; Mary; the Jews who had come to mourn
settings.to: Martha to Mary privately; Mary to Jesus at the place outside the village; the mourners among themselves
settings.when: right after Jesus' talk with Martha, with the mourners from Jerusalem following Mary
settings.why: Martha calls Mary quietly, perhaps to spare Jesus the crowd. Mary repeats her sister's words (11:21, 32) but with tears and at his feet, and Jesus answers her not with teaching but with anger at death and tears. The mourners' two remarks (11:36–37) show the split the sign will cause: some see his love, others doubt his power.
settings.readers: For the Gospel's readers this scene showed that Jesus meets grief with grief before he meets it with power.

settings.what: Jesus' prayer of thanks at the tomb and his command to Lazarus
settings.to: the Father, aloud, in the hearing of the sisters and the crowd of mourners from Jerusalem; then to Lazarus and the bystanders
settings.when: at the opened tomb, after Martha's protest about the smell
settings.why: The prayer makes clear to the crowd that what is about to happen is the Father's answer, done through the one he sent, so they may believe (11:42). The command shows Jesus' voice giving life (5:25), and the order to untie Lazarus brings the bystanders into the sign.
settings.readers: For the Gospel's readers the loud voice at the tomb was a foretaste of the last day, when "everyone lying in the tombs will hear his voice" (5:28).

settings.what: The council's plot and Caiaphas' words
settings.by: the chief priests and Pharisees in council; Caiaphas the high priest
settings.to: the members of the council meeting in Jerusalem
settings.when: soon after the raising of Lazarus, a few weeks before Passover, probably AD 30 or 33
settings.why: The council's aim is political survival: to stop a movement that could bring Roman reprisals against the temple and the nation. Caiaphas' words are meant to end the debate with hard-headed advice, one life for many. John adds that, without knowing it, the high priest prophesied the saving meaning of Jesus' death.
settings.readers: Readers after AD 70 knew that Rome had destroyed the temple anyway. They would feel the irony: the plan meant to save "our place" did not save it, while the death it caused gathered God's scattered children into one.
views: Many scholars, including some Jewish historians, find a private council decision before Passover, driven by fear of Rome, historically likely, and some prefer it to the Synoptic night trial.
Others think John composed the meeting to explain Jesus' death through the gift of life, and to give his theology of substitution a speaker (11:50–52).

traditions.q: When Jesus calls death "sleep" (11:11–14), do the dead sleep until the resurrection, or are they consciously with God?
views: The soul is immortal and is judged at death. It enters heaven, at once or after purification in purgatory, or is lost; at the resurrection it will be reunited with the body (Catechism 1005, 1021–1022, 1030). Catholic teachers explain "sleep" as a picture of how death looks to the living, not as unconsciousness.

At death the soul goes to a foretaste of joy or sorrow, awaiting the final judgment and the resurrection of the body (Confession of Dositheus, decree 18). The church prays for the departed and keeps Lazarus Saturday as a promise of the general resurrection.

Luther often spoke of death as a deep sleep from which believers wake at the last day as if from a moment's rest (Lectures on Genesis), yet he held that the soul lives before God. Later Lutheran theology, as in Francis Pieper's dogmatics, teaches that believers' souls are with Christ while they await the resurrection.

At death the souls of believers, "which neither die nor sleep," return to God; "the souls of the righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens" to wait for the redemption of their bodies (Westminster Confession 32.1). "Sleep" refers to the body.
The same as the Reformed view in the Second London Confession (31.1): believers' souls go at once to be with Christ, and their bodies rest until the resurrection.

Death is an unconscious state for all people; the dead do not go to heaven or hell at death but rest until the resurrection. Jesus' words about Lazarus' "sleep" (11:11–14) are a key text for this teaching (Fundamental Belief 26).

Humans do not have an immortal soul; at death a person ceases to exist and is conscious of nothing. The resurrection is God's re-creating the person, as Lazarus' raising pictures (Insight on the Scriptures, articles "Death" and "Soul").

title: The Hour Has Come
sum: Six days before Passover, at a supper in Bethany, Mary pours a pound of costly nard on Jesus' feet and wipes them with her hair. Judas protests that the money should have gone to the poor, and John says he was a thief. Jesus defends her: it is for the day of his burial. The crowds come to see Lazarus, and the chief priests plan to kill him too. The next day the festival crowd meets Jesus with palm branches, shouting "Hosanna!" and hailing him as the King of Israel, and Jesus rides in on a young donkey, as Zechariah foretold.

When some Greeks ask to see him, Jesus announces that his hour has come. A grain of wheat must die to bear fruit. His soul is shaken, but he will not ask to be spared, and a voice from heaven answers his prayer to glorify the Father's name. Once lifted up, he says, he will draw everyone to himself. John then closes Jesus' public ministry with a verdict, quoting Isaiah to explain why so many did not believe, and with a final summary of Jesus' message: whoever sees him sees the one who sent him; he came not to judge but to save.
readings: Read as the end of the public ministry

Chapter 12 closes the first half of John. The signs are over (12:37), the light hides itself (12:36), and the narrator looks back with Isaiah to explain the unbelief. Read this way, the chapter is a summing up: the anointing points to burial, the entry to kingship, the Greeks to the world-wide harvest, and 12:44–50 gathers the main themes of Jesus' teaching.

Mary anoints, the crowd hails a king, Zechariah's king rides in on a donkey, and Jesus speaks of being "lifted up." Read this way, the chapter is a coronation, but a strange one: the anointing is for burial, the throne is a cross, and the king's victory is over "this world's ruler."

John's anointing and entry have parallels in Matthew 21 and 26, Mark 11 and 14, and Luke 7 and 19, and 12:27 holds what the others place in Gethsemane. Read side by side, the differences show each Gospel's interests: John alone names Mary and Judas' objection, mentions palms, places the donkey after the acclamation, and has the Greeks come.

views.H: John's chronology puts the supper about the Sabbath before Passover and the entry on a Sunday, the source of Palm Sunday. Palms carried in welcome recalled the Maccabees' victories, and Roman authorities watched festival crowds closely. Gentile God-fearers could worship only in the outer court of the temple. Bethsaida, home of Philip and Andrew, lay in a mostly Greek-speaking area.
views.C: Most scholars think John's anointing story combines elements found in Mark 14:3–9 (Bethany, nard, three hundred denarii, burial) and Luke 7:36–50 (feet, hair), either by knowing those Gospels or through shared oral tradition. Many see 12:44–50 as a summary placed here by the evangelist or an editor, since Jesus has just withdrawn (12:36). 12:27–28 is often read as John's version of the Gethsemane tradition.
views.L: The chapter is built of contrasts: Mary's lavish love and Judas' greed, the crowd's "King of Israel" and the humble donkey, the Pharisees' "the world has gone after him" and the Greeks who come, glory from people and glory from God (12:43). The long-awaited "hour" finally arrives (12:23), and "lifted up" carries both cross and exaltation.
views.J: The crowd sings Psalm 118, part of the Hallel sung at Passover, and waves palms as at the Festival of Shelters and the Hanukkah rededication. Jesus' saying on the grain of wheat has a close rabbinic parallel about the resurrection. 12:37–43 blames the unbelief of many on God's hardening, quoting Isaiah 6, and Jewish readers have rightly asked how the passage has been used: as a statement about some of Jesus' hearers, or as a verdict on Israel. Romans 11 insists that such hardening is partial and temporary.
views.T: Western readers had to explain the Vulgate's "I will draw all things to myself"; Augustine took "all" as all kinds of people (Tractates on John 52.11). Palm Sunday processions, described by the pilgrim Egeria in Jerusalem in the 380s, re-enact 12:12–15. Augustine read 12:24–25 as a law of the Christian life, and the saying has been a favorite text of martyrs and missionaries.

Most scholars think Mark, Matthew and John tell one event, though the dates differ (two days or six days before Passover). Luke's story differs in setting, meaning and time, and many think it was a separate event that came to share details with the Bethany story as the stories were retold. See the notes on 11:2 and 12:3.

deep.h: The entry into Jerusalem in four Gospels
deep.b: All four Gospels tell of Jesus' entry into Jerusalem on a donkey before his last Passover (Matthew 21:1–11; Mark 11:1–11; Luke 19:28–40; John 12:12–19). They agree on the donkey, the crowd, and the shout from Psalm 118:25–26. They differ in detail. In the other three, Jesus sends two disciples to fetch the animal; John says only that he "found" it. Matthew alone has two animals and quotes Zechariah at length; John also quotes Zechariah 9:9, in short form. Mark has leafy branches, Matthew branches from trees, Luke cloaks only; John alone has palms. Mark and Luke have "the coming kingdom of our father David" and "the King"; John has "the King of Israel." Only John says the crowd came out from Jerusalem because of Lazarus (12:17–18), and only John admits that the disciples did not understand until later (12:16). In Mark, Jesus then goes into the temple and the next day drives out the traders; in John that happened at the first Passover (2:13–22).

deep.h: "They were unable to believe": Isaiah and John's verdict
deep.b:
12:37–43 is the narrator's own comment at the end of Jesus' public work. It quotes two passages of Isaiah. The first (Isaiah 53:1) shows that the prophet foresaw unbelief in the message of God's servant. The second (Isaiah 6:10) says God blinded eyes and hardened hearts. John then says, startlingly, that Isaiah "saw his glory," Christ's (12:41).

Three points help a fair reading. First, the early Christians used these and similar verses to face a painful fact: most of Jesus' own people did not believe in him (Mark 4:12; Acts 28:25–28; Romans 10:16; 11:8). The texts are an explanation from within Scripture, not a verdict that Israel is finished; Paul says the hardening is partial and temporary (Romans 11:25–26). Second, John at once adds that "many even among the rulers did believe" (12:42). Third, John does not remove human responsibility: those who reject Jesus' word are judged by it (12:48). How God's hardening and human choice fit together is debated (see the card below).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the Greeks get their answer at the cross
deep.b: The Greeks ask, "Sir, we want to see Jesus" (12:21), and then disappear from the story. Jesus never seems to answer them. My suggestion is that John means the whole speech, and finally the cross, to be the answer. Jesus says that the grain must die before there is fruit (12:24) and that once lifted up he will draw everyone (12:32). Seven chapters later, the notice over the cross is written "in Hebrew, in Latin and in Greek" (19:20), so that Greeks too can read who the crucified man is, and the soldiers and passers-by "will look at the one they pierced" (19:37). On this reading, the Greeks will "see Jesus" when he is lifted up, not before. Many commentators (Brown, Carson, Lincoln) note that the Greeks' coming signals the hour and the Gentile mission; the link to the Greek inscription and to "seeing" at the cross is my own extension, and it is a reading, not something the text states.

echoes: Matthew 21:1–11; Matthew 26:6–13; Mark 11:1–11; Mark 14:3–9; Luke 7:36–50; Luke 19:28–40; Psalm 118:25–26; Zechariah 9:9; Zephaniah 3:14–16; Deuteronomy 15:11; Isaiah 52:13; Isaiah 53:1; Isaiah 6:9–10; Psalm 89:36; Mark 14:32–36; 3:14; 8:28; 19:20; Romans 11:7–10

settings.what: Judas' complaint and Jesus' defense of Mary
settings.to: the guests at the supper in Bethany: the disciples, Lazarus, Martha and Mary
settings.when: at the supper six days before Passover, just after Mary anoints Jesus' feet
settings.why: Judas' words sound like concern for the poor, but John says they hid his theft. Jesus' answer protects Mary from shame before the guests and gives her act its meaning: it belongs to his burial. His saying about the poor, from Deuteronomy 15:11, reminds the hearers that giving to the poor never ends, while his time with them is short.
settings.readers: For the Gospel's readers Mary became a model of lavish love for Jesus, and Judas a warning that pious words about the poor can hide greed.
views: Mark places the objection on the lips of "some" and adds that the woman's deed will be told in her memory (Mark 14:4–9). Many think John has named the objector to sharpen the contrast between two disciples.

settings.what: The crowd's welcome from Psalm 118, Zechariah's prophecy, and the Pharisees' complaint
settings.by: the festival crowd; the narrator quoting Zechariah; the Pharisees
settings.to: Jesus, as he approaches Jerusalem; the Pharisees to one another
settings.when: the day after the supper, about five days before Passover, as pilgrims fill the city
settings.why: The crowd's shout is meant to welcome Jesus as the king who comes in the Lord's name, the national deliverer. The Zechariah quotation corrects that hope: this king comes on a donkey, gently. The Pharisees' complaint shows the leaders' helplessness and, without their knowing it, announces the coming of the Greeks.
settings.readers: The Gospel's readers knew that the king the crowd welcomed would be crucified within the week, and that his kingdom "does not come from this world" (18:36).

settings.what: Jesus' answer to the Greeks' request: the hour, the grain of wheat, and being lifted up
settings.by: Jesus, with a voice from heaven (12:28)
settings.to: Philip and Andrew, and through them the Greeks; then the crowd in Jerusalem
settings.when: during the days before Passover, probably in the temple courts, after Greek God-fearers ask to see him
settings.why: The Greeks' request tells Jesus that the time has come for his death to bear fruit for the world. He explains it to his followers (the grain must die; whoever serves him must follow), faces his own fear openly, and calls the crowd to believe in the light while they still have it. The speech is meant to turn a request for a meeting into a call to faith in a crucified Messiah.
settings.readers: Readers late in the first century, among them Gentiles who had come to faith, could see themselves in the Greeks who asked to see Jesus and in the "lot of fruit" the buried grain produces.

settings.what: The narrator's verdict on the unbelief, with Isaiah 53:1 and 6:10
settings.when: at the close of Jesus' public ministry, looking back over the signs
settings.why: To answer a question that troubled the first Christians: if Jesus did so many signs, why did so many of his own people not believe? John finds the answer in Isaiah, and in the fear of men among those who did believe (12:42–43).
settings.readers: For the Gospel's readers, at a time when believers in Jesus and the synagogue were drawing apart, the passage explained why many of Jesus' own people had not believed, and warned believers against loving human approval.
views: Most interpreters read it as about the unbelief of many of Jesus' contemporaries, not a judgment on the Jewish people for all time.
Some read 12:39–40 as teaching that God's hardening makes unbelief certain; others stress that it follows persistent refusal (12:37) and that it is partial (12:42).
Readers put out of the synagogue

J. Louis Martyn and many after him read the passage, with 12:42, as written for a community recently expelled from the synagogue; others doubt that setting and think John wrote for churches in general (Richard Bauckham).

settings.to: the people of Jerusalem in general, as a summary of what he had said in public
settings.when: John gives no time or place; Jesus has just withdrawn (12:36), so most see these words as a summary of his public teaching placed here as an epilogue
settings.why: To restate, one last time, the heart of Jesus' message: he is sent by the Father, he is light for the world, he came to save and not to judge, and his word is the Father's command that brings eternal life. Those who reject it are not judged by Jesus' anger but by the word itself.
settings.readers: For the Gospel's readers these verses gathered the whole public message in brief, a last invitation before the private chapters of the supper begin.
views: Brown and most scholars think John or a later editor gathered key sayings here to close the public ministry.
A real speech at another time
Some interpreters take it as words Jesus spoke on another occasion, reported here because they sum up his public teaching.

traditions.q: When Jesus says, "I will draw everyone to myself" (12:32), and John says some "were unable to believe" (12:39–40), does God draw every person, and can people refuse?
views: God wills all people to be saved and gives every person grace sufficient for salvation; people can freely refuse it. God predestines no one to hell (Catechism 1037). The Council of Trent taught that the free will moved by grace can assent or refuse.

Christ draws all; salvation is a cooperation (synergy) between God's grace and human freedom, which can accept or refuse grace (Confession of Dositheus, decree 14). Hardening in Scripture follows people's own refusal. Some fathers, such as Gregory of Nyssa, hoped all might finally be restored, but Origen's teaching of universal restoration was condemned in 553.
God's grace is offered to all in Word and sacrament, and it can be resisted; yet those saved are saved by grace alone, and no one is chosen for damnation (Formula of Concord, article 11).

"Everyone" means the children of God, Calvin wrote on this verse, and with Chrysostom he added that it takes in Gentiles as well as Jews, as the coming of the Greeks shows. The drawing of the elect is effective and is not finally refused (Canons of Dort, heads 3–4); 12:39–40 shows that God justly leaves others in their unbelief.

By prevenient grace Christ draws every person, enabling all to respond; grace can be resisted. Wesley preached that God's grace is "free in all and free for all" and rejected unconditional reprobation.

Divided. Many Baptists hold that Christ draws all and that each person must freely respond; Reformed Baptists, following the Second London Confession, read the drawing as effectual calling of the elect.
